section.title: The Coming Darkness
section.sectionRationale: This movement continues the Immanuel oracles by naming a second sign-child, Maher-shalal-hash-baz, dating the coming Assyrian devastation precisely, then pivots to the flood imagery of Assyria overwhelming even Immanuel's own land, before closing with a call to fear the LORD alone rather than conspiracies and mediums, ending in a picture of a people wandering in darkness and distress.
section.thesis: Because Judah rejected the gently flowing waters of Shiloah for fear of foreign kings, the LORD will bring the flood of Assyria upon them, yet He remains a sanctuary for those who fear Him rightly, even while He is a stone of stumbling for a disbelieving nation groping in darkness.
section.frameNote: Four movements: the naming and dating of the sign-child Maher-shalal-hash-baz; the flood of Assyria reaching to Immanuel's own neck; the call to fear the LORD alone rather than conspiracy and divination; and the closing picture of darkness for those who reject His word.

units.label: Maher-shalal-hash-baz
units.note: a sign-child dating the coming devastation

verses.text: Then the LORD said to me, “Take a large scroll and write on it with an ordinary stylus: Maher-shalal-hash-baz.
And I will appoint for Myself trustworthy witnesses, Uriah the priest and Zechariah son of Jeberekiah.”
And I had relations with the prophetess, and she conceived and gave birth to a son. The LORD said to me, “Name him Maher-shalal-hash-baz.
For before the boy knows how to cry ‘Father’ or ‘Mother,’ the wealth of Damascus and the plunder of Samaria will be carried off by the king of Assyria.”

units.label: The flood of Assyria
units.note: waters reaching even to the neck

verses.text: And the LORD spoke to me further:
“Because this people has rejected the gently flowing waters of Shiloah and rejoiced in Rezin and the son of Remaliah,

the Lord will surely bring against them the mighty floodwaters of the Euphrates, the king of Assyria and all his pomp. 
It will overflow its channels and overrun its banks.

It will pour into Judah, swirling and sweeping over it, 
reaching up to the neck; its spreading streams will cover your entire land, O Immanuel!
Huddle together, O peoples, and be shattered; pay attention, all you distant lands; prepare for battle, and be shattered; prepare for battle, and be shattered!

Devise a plan, but it will be thwarted; state a proposal, but it will not happen. 
For God is with us. ”

units.label: Fear the LORD alone
units.note: a sanctuary, or a stone of stumbling

verses.text: For this is what the LORD has spoken to me with a strong hand, instructing me not to walk in the way of this people:
“Do not call conspiracy everything these people regard as conspiracy. Do not fear what they fear; do not live in dread.
The LORD of Hosts is the One you shall regard as holy. Only He should be feared; only He should be dreaded.
And He will be a {{miqdash|sanctuary}}, but to both houses of Israel a stone of stumbling and a rock of offense, to the dwellers of Jerusalem a trap and a snare.

Many will stumble over these; they will fall and be broken; 
they will be ensnared and captured.”
Bind up the testimony and seal the {{torah2|law}} among my disciples.

I will wait for the LORD, who is hiding His face from the house of Jacob. 
I will put my trust in Him.
Here am I, and the children the LORD has given me as signs and symbols in Israel from the LORD of Hosts, who dwells on Mount Zion.

units.label: Darkness for a disbelieving people
units.note: to the law and to the testimony

verses.text: When men tell you to consult the spirits of the dead and the spiritists who whisper and mutter, shouldn't a people consult their God instead? Why consult the dead on behalf of the living?
To the law and to the testimony! If they do not speak according to this word, they have no light of dawn.
They will roam the land, dejected and hungry. When they are famished, they will become enraged; and looking upward, they will curse their king and their God.
Then they will look to the earth and see only distress and darkness and the gloom of anguish. And they will be driven into utter darkness.

miqdash.gloss: Sanctuary, holy place, a refuge in God's own presence. The LORD is a miqdash to those who fear Him rightly, yet the very same LORD becomes a stone of stumbling to a nation that will not trust Him, an image Paul and Peter both apply directly to Christ, Romans 9:33, 1 Peter 2:8.

torah2.gloss: Instruction, teaching, law. Isaiah is told to bind up and seal this testimony among his disciples, preserving God's authoritative word for a future when it would be vindicated, and the phrase 'to the law and to the testimony' in verse 20 becomes a timeless standard for testing every claim to truth.

basic.context: Isaiah is told to name his second son Maher-shalal-hash-baz, quick to the plunder, swift to the spoil, dating precisely how soon Damascus and Samaria would fall to Assyria. But then the chapter warns that the very Assyrian flood meant to remove Judah's enemies will instead overrun Judah itself, reaching up to the neck, right up to Immanuel's own land. In the middle of this crisis, God calls His people to fear Him alone rather than conspiracy theories or mediums, promising to be either a sanctuary or a stumbling stone depending on how people respond, and the chapter closes with a stark image of a people wandering in hunger, rage, and utter darkness because they refused His word.
basic.hermeneutics: This is a real, dated prophecy tied to actual political events, the fall of Damascus and Samaria to Assyria within a few short years, so its short-term accuracy grounds confidence in Isaiah's longer-range promises. The uncomfortable question is why God would become a stumbling stone to His own people; the answer is that the same truth that saves those who trust it necessarily judges those who reject it, a pattern the New Testament applies directly to Christ Himself.
basic.originalLanguages: The LORD promises to be a miqdash, sanctuary, to those who rightly fear Him, yet a stone of stumbling to a disbelieving nation, the same object producing opposite effects depending on the heart's response. Isaiah is told to bind up the testimony and seal the torah, instruction, among his disciples, preserving God's word for later vindication even while contemporaries reject it.
basic.typology: The LORD as sanctuary to some and stumbling stone to others directly anticipates Christ, whom Paul and Peter both explicitly identify as this very stone, a rock of offense to unbelief yet the sure foundation and refuge for those who trust Him. The sign-children given to Isaiah, walking testimonies of God's coming judgment and salvation, foreshadow how God continues to use ordinary lives as living signs of His purposes.
basic.christ: Romans 9:32-33 and 1 Peter 2:6-8 both quote this very passage, Isaiah 8:14, identifying Christ Himself as the stone that is a sanctuary of refuge to believers but a stumbling block to those who reject Him in unbelief. Just as Immanuel's own land would be overrun by the flood in this chapter, Christ, God with us, enters fully into human suffering and judgment, so that those who trust Him find in Him the sanctuary Isaiah promised rather than the stumbling stone.
basic.god: God is sovereign over international events, precisely dating Assyria's conquests, yet He is also intimately near, present as Immanuel even amid the devastation He sends as discipline. He calls His people away from fear of circumstance and occult manipulation toward fear of Him alone, promising that the same LORD who judges the unbelieving is a sure refuge for those who trust Him.
basic.crossReferences: 2 Kings 17:1-6 and 2 Kings 16 narrate the historical fall of Samaria and Damascus this chapter anticipates. Romans 9:32-33 identifies Christ as the stone of stumbling from this very passage. 1 Peter 2:6-8 develops the same stone imagery, a precious cornerstone to believers, a stumbling stone to unbelievers. Deuteronomy 18:10-11 forbids the very consultation of mediums and spiritists this chapter warns against.
basic.oneStory: Isaiah 8 shows that God's word always produces one of two outcomes: sanctuary for those who trust it, and stumbling for those who reject it in favor of fear and superstition. That same dividing stone becomes explicit in Christ, in whom trust finds refuge and unbelief finds only offense, and the whole story moves toward everyone eventually facing that same choice.

context.literary:
Isaiah 8 is built from small units that turn on one word, and the word is often a name. The chapter begins with a name written on a scroll, Maher-shalal-hash-baz, verses 1 to 4. It goes on to the name Immanuel, which surfaces twice more, in verses 8 and 10, as the address of a land and as a reason to be unafraid. It closes with a family of names, 'Here am I, and the children the LORD has given me as signs and symbols,' verse 18, and the prophet's own name, which means 'the LORD saves,' stands behind them all. In this chapter Isaiah's household is the sermon.

The movement is from flood to refuge to darkness. The first half is the water: the gentle stream of Shiloah rejected, the Euphrates risen and overflowing, and the nations told to huddle and be shattered, verses 5 to 10. The middle is the fear of the LORD, introduced by the strong hand of verse 11, with the paired threat and refuge of verses 13 and 14, and the sealing of the testimony in verse 16. The close is the descent into the dark, verses 19 to 22, set against the one light that remains, the instruction and the testimony of verse 20.

There is a deliberate echo of chapter 7. The sign child of the earlier chapter is answered by a second child in chapter 8, and both carry a timetable in terms of a boy's early development, 7:16 and 8:4. The flood of 8:7 develops the razor of 7:20, and the 'you who are Immanuel's land' of 8:8 uses the name that 7:14 gave as a promise. The end of the chapter also prepares the next: the words about darkness and distress in verse 22 are overturned in 9:1-2, 'The people walking in darkness have seen a great light.' What looks like a closing is really the lowest point before a turn.
context.historical:
The events belong to the years of the Syro-Ephraimite war, about 734 to 732 BC. Isaiah is told to write on a large scroll with 'an ordinary stylus,' literally a man's stylus, in clear ordinary script, so that all can read the name. He is to have two reliable witnesses, Uriah the priest and Zechariah son of Jeberekiah, verse 2. A priest named Uriah appears in 2 Kings 16:10-16 as the man who built the altar copied from Damascus at Ahaz's orders. If this is the same man, the LORD chooses as a witness to the prophecy someone who is in the king's pocket, and thus makes his testimony hard to deny when events prove it right.

The interval named in verse 4 was short. Before the boy could say 'Father' or 'Mother,' perhaps a year or two, Assyria moved. 2 Kings 15:29 records that Tiglath-pileser captured Galilee and all the land of Naphtali, and 2 Kings 16:9 that he took Damascus and put Rezin to death. The spoil of Damascus and Samaria were carried off as the sign had said. The same Assyrian king who rescued Ahaz from his two enemies then became the flood.

The waters of Shiloah are the spring that fed Jerusalem through its channel, quiet and small, a spring that comes out of the city's own hill. The 'mighty floodwaters of the Euphrates' are the opposite: a great river from Assyria's side of the world, bringing its king and all his pomp. The contrast is between a small, steady, local source that belongs to God's city, and an overpowering one that arrives from outside.

The practices of verse 19 are the old Near Eastern ways of seeking guidance from the dead. They were forbidden to Israel in Leviticus 19:31, 20:6 and Deuteronomy 18:10-12, but were never far away, as the story of King Saul at Endor shows, 1 Samuel 28:7-8. A court anxious about invasion would be tempted by them, as by an alliance with Assyria.
context.canonical:
The chapter has one of the most important stone passages in Scripture. Isaiah 8:14 names the LORD as a stone of stumbling and rock of offense. Isaiah 28:16 goes further: 'See, I lay a stone in Zion, a tested stone, a precious cornerstone, a sure foundation; the one who believes will never be shaken.' And Psalm 118:22 says, 'The stone the builders rejected has become the cornerstone.' The New Testament weaves these three together. Romans 9:32-33 joins Isaiah 8:14 and 28:16 for Israel's stumbling over Christ. 1 Peter 2:6-8 puts the three side by side. Jesus Himself uses Psalm 118 and then adds a warning that echoes the stone of stumbling, 'He who falls on this stone will be broken to pieces,' Matthew 21:42-44. Simeon says that this child is 'appointed to cause the rise and fall of many in Israel,' Luke 2:34.

The call to fear the LORD alone is applied in 1 Peter 3:14-15. Peter quotes the Greek of Isaiah 8:12, 'Do not fear what they fear; do not be shaken,' and in the next verse, 'sanctify Christ as Lord,' he echoes Isaiah 8:13, where it is the LORD of hosts whom they are to regard as holy. In Peter's use the title that Isaiah gave to the LORD is given to Christ.

The prophet's words in verses 17 and 18, 'I will put my trust in Him' and 'Here am I, and the children God has given me,' are put on the lips of Christ in Hebrews 2:13, which says that Jesus is not ashamed to call His people brothers, Hebrews 2:11.

The darkness of verse 22 is answered in the next chapter and then the Gospels. Isaiah 9:1-2 promises light to the same regions, Zebulun and Naphtali, and Matthew 4:12-16 shows Jesus beginning His ministry in Capernaum to fulfil it. Luke 1:78-79 and John 1:5, 'The Light shines in the darkness, and the darkness has not overcome it,' belong to the same line.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Isaiah wanted the people of Jerusalem to read their own history through the child he had named and the scroll he had published. A dated, witnessed prophecy leaves no room for later claims that the prophet only saw things afterward. When Damascus and Samaria fell within the time of a boy's early childhood, Judah had proof that Isaiah had spoken for the LORD, and the same prophet's warning about Assyria's flood would carry the same weight.

He also meant to warn that the way of safety was not the way of the crowd. The commanded stance of verses 11 to 13 is to see the world differently, not merely to act differently. 'Do not call conspiracy everything these people regard as conspiracy' is an instruction about what to take seriously. The one who is truly to be feared is not the coalition of Rezin and Pekah, but the LORD. Fear of God drives out fear of men, and the fear that Judah had of its enemies exposed how little they feared Him.

The closing verses are a plea. When people tell Judah to consult the dead, Isaiah answers that a people should consult their God, and that the place to do so is the written word. The sealing of the testimony among his disciples, verse 16, shows that he expected rejection and meant his words to wait for a day when they would be vindicated. A faithful remnant would keep what the nation despised.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The flood, the darkness and the roaming hunger are descriptions of what the LORD said would happen to a particular people at a particular time. They are not an instruction to read every political upheaval as a flood on an unfaithful nation. The prophecy is tied to named kings and dated events, and its authority rests on that connection.

The commands of the chapter do carry forward, however. 'Do not fear what they fear' and 'Only He should be feared' are given to the faithful as an instruction, and Peter applies them to Christians who suffer, 1 Peter 3:14-15. The question of verse 19, 'shouldn't a people consult their God instead?', still applies to anyone who looks for guidance in forbidden sources, and the answer, 'To the law and to the testimony!' is a rule that Scripture is the measure of every claim to speak for God. It does not follow that every uncomfortable sermon proves the speaker is right; the test is whether what is said agrees with 'this word,' verse 20. And the promise that the LORD will be a sanctuary to those who fear Him is an invitation, not a guarantee made to a nation by default, Isaiah 66:2.

debates.question: What is the refusal of 'the gently flowing waters of Shiloah'?

views.label: Rejecting the house of David and its God given rule
views.case: The spring that served Jerusalem is a quiet symbol of the LORD's protection of the city and the Davidic line. Judah rejects this by preferring fear of the coalition, or a more impressive Assyrian help. The contrast between small and gentle waters and an overflowing river fits the contrast between trust in God and trust in the empire. This is the most common reading.

views.label: Rejecting Isaiah's message of quiet trust
views.case: Isaiah had just told Ahaz to 'calm down and be quiet,' Isaiah 7:4. The gentle waters stand for that quiet confidence. Isaiah 30:15 says, 'By repentance and rest you would be saved; your strength would lie in quiet confidence,' and then, 'you were not willing.' On this view the people who rejoiced in Rezin and Pekah were people who found the gentle way of trust too slow.

views.label: A literal reference to a political choice
views.case: Some think the 'people' who reject Shiloah are northern Israelites who preferred the alliance with Rezin to loyalty to David's house, so that the flood falls first on the north. Verse 8 then says it will pass into Judah also.

debates.bearing: All three views agree on the shape: a small and steady provision of God is despised, and a great and violent power takes its place. The flood is what the people have chosen, and in each reading the remedy is the same, to trust the LORD's quiet help.

debates.question: How does the child of verse 3 relate to Immanuel in Isaiah 7:14?

views.label: The child of 8:3 is the fulfilment of 7:14
views.case: The 'prophetess' becomes pregnant and bears a son in the immediate context, with a timetable that matches 7:16, 'before the boy knows enough to reject evil and choose good.' Immanuel and Maher-shalal-hash-baz would then be two names of one child, a name of hope and a name of judgment. This explains why chapter 8 calls the land 'Immanuel's.'

views.label: Two separate signs, with Immanuel still to come
views.case: Isaiah 8:3 is a sign about the plunder of Damascus and Samaria, and it gives a different name. The mother in 7:14 is called 'the young woman' and the child will be named by the mother, whereas in chapter 8 the LORD tells Isaiah the name. The two timetables are alike but the births are separate, and Immanuel, who is addressed in verse 8 as the owner of the land, is the Davidic child who points to the future.

views.label: Both belong to a pattern of signs
views.case: Isaiah says in verse 18 that he and his children are 'signs and symbols in Israel,' so each child has a role. Shear-jashub is a remnant, Maher-shalal-hash-baz is judgment on enemies, and Immanuel is God's presence. Together they form a pattern of signs.

debates.bearing: The text does not say that the two are the same, and it does not say they are different. Matthew's use of Isaiah 7:14 for Jesus is not affected: whatever child came first in Isaiah's day, the name Immanuel in 8:8 and 8:10 still stretches beyond that child to the land and the people and, in the end, to Christ.

study.originalLanguages:
The long name of verse 1, Maher-shalal-hash-baz, is made of two pairs of near synonyms for plunder: maher and chash both carry the sense of hurrying, and shalal and baz both mean spoil or prey. The BSB footnote gives 'The spoil speeds, the prey hastens' and 'Swift to plunder, quick to carry away.' It is a whole sentence used as a name. A child will carry a message in his name, and the name will be said at every roll call and every meal.

The command to write on a large scroll uses a word for tablet or scroll, gillayon, and the stylus is 'a man's stylus,' as the footnote says, in ordinary letters that any reader could follow. The point is public accessibility. Verse 2 adds the witnesses, a legal move, so that the prophecy is placed on record before it can come true.

The people have 'rejected' the waters of Shiloah, and the verb ma'as means to refuse and despise, the verb Isaiah 5:24 uses of rejecting the instruction of the LORD. The same word describes the people's rejection of the quiet stream and of the word of God. The verb for the flood in verse 8, shataph, 'overflow, sweep along,' is the verb used for a river bursting its banks, and the flood climbs 'up to the neck,' literally reaches the neck, so that the land is nearly submerged but not drowned. A body in water up to its neck can still breathe, which is the grace inside the judgment. The same hint is behind the preservation of Judah when Assyria later fails to take Jerusalem, Isaiah 37:35.

Verse 8's cry 'O Immanuel' is the same Hebrew name as in 7:14, but here it is a form of address to the land. In verse 10, the footnote says, 'Hebrew Immanuel,' so the phrase 'God is with us' is the name itself, said as a defiance of every plan against it.

In verse 12 the word for 'conspiracy' is qesher. The people see plots everywhere, and the prophet is told not to share their dread. In verse 13 the verb 'regard as holy' is the causative of qadash, to make holy or treat as holy, the same root as the 'Holy One of Israel' and the cry of the seraphim in 6:3. To sanctify the LORD is to give Him the place in the heart that His holiness deserves, and Peter takes the same verb in 1 Peter 3:15. 'Fear' and 'dread' are two words for the awe that belongs to Him alone.

The noun miqdash, 'sanctuary,' is from the same root as 'holy.' A sanctuary is a holy place, and one runs into it for safety. Set beside it are 'stone of stumbling' and 'rock of offense' and the paired hunting terms 'trap' and 'snare.' The one holy LORD is a refuge or an obstacle according to the response.

In verse 16 the words 'testimony' and 'law' are te'udah and torah. The first is what is attested or bears witness, and the second is instruction. The command to bind and seal is a picture of a document tied and stamped to preserve it, as Jeremiah's scroll was preserved in Jeremiah 36:2-4. In verse 20 they come back, 'To the law and to the testimony!', as the two words that stand against the whispering of the mediums.

The mediums of verse 19 are described with the words ovot and yidde'onim, 'spirits of the dead' and 'spiritists,' the same pair as in Leviticus 19:31 and Deuteronomy 18:11, and their speech is called a 'whisper and mutter,' the chirping of something that cannot give a clear word. Isaiah 29:4 uses the same picture, 'your speech will whisper out of the dust.' The final phrase of verse 22, 'driven into utter darkness,' uses a passive form of the verb for being driven or scattered: the people who cannot find their way are pushed into it.

typology.type: The stone of stumbling and sanctuary, Isaiah 8:14
typology.fulfillment: The same LORD is a sanctuary to the trusting and a stumbling stone to the unbelieving. Paul applies the verse to Israel's response to Christ, Romans 9:32-33, joining it to Isaiah 28:16, and Peter does the same in 1 Peter 2:6-8, adding Psalm 118:22. Jesus Himself speaks of the stone that crushes those it falls on, Matthew 21:44. The correspondence is exact in structure: one object, two outcomes, by faith or unbelief. The escalation is that the LORD of hosts is now seen in a person, and the stumbling is over the cross. The type falls short in one respect only: 'the one who believes in Him will never be put to shame,' Romans 9:33, so the sanctuary promise is carried further than the Old Testament text states.

typology.type: The prophet and the children given to him, Isaiah 8:17-18
typology.fulfillment: Isaiah stands before the LORD with children who are signs, and says that he will trust the LORD who hides His face. Hebrews 2:13 puts these words on the lips of Christ: 'I will put My trust in Him,' and 'Here am I, and the children God has given Me.' The correspondence is between a prophet who identifies with his household and a Saviour who identifies with those He saves, who, 'since the children have flesh and blood,' also 'shared in their humanity,' Hebrews 2:14. The type falls short because Isaiah's children were signs of judgment and hope, while Christ's children are brought to glory, Hebrews 2:10.

The quiet spring that God provided in Jerusalem is the pool called Siloam. John records that Jesus sent a blind man to wash in the Pool of Siloam, and adds the translation of the name, 'Sent,' John 9:7. The man received sight, and Jesus said that He came 'so that the blind may see and those who see may become blind,' John 9:39, the same pattern of sight and blindness that runs through Isaiah 6 to 8. This is a link of place and theme, not a claim that Isaiah meant it. It shows that the gentle waters were the LORD's own provision, and that rejecting it was rejecting Him.

The picture of anguish and darkness in the land of Naphtali is answered in Isaiah 9:1-2 by a great light on the same region. Matthew says that this is fulfilled when Jesus settles in Capernaum, in Zebulun and Naphtali, Matthew 4:12-16. John says, 'The Light shines in the darkness, and the darkness has not overcome it,' John 1:5. The correspondence is geographic and moral. The escalation is the arrival of a person who is the light. The type falls short in that Isaiah's darkness was the political and spiritual night of Assyrian invasion, while Christ's light shines on a darkness that includes sin and death, Luke 1:78-79.

study.christ:
The most direct link is the stone. Isaiah 8:14 says of the LORD of hosts, 'He will be a sanctuary, but to both houses of Israel a stone of stumbling and a rock of offense.' Paul quotes it, merged with Isaiah 28:16, to explain why Israel did not attain the righteousness it pursued: 'They stumbled over the stumbling stone,' Romans 9:32. Peter quotes it with the cornerstone of Psalm 118 and says that the stone is precious to those who believe and a stone of stumbling to those who do not, 1 Peter 2:6-8. In both passages the stone is Christ, and the pronoun in the quotation, 'the one who believes in Him,' is placed on the stone. The apostles read the title of the LORD of hosts as one that Jesus bears. Because the Old Testament text says that the LORD Himself is the stone, the New Testament identification carries the same weight as the claim that Jesus is the LORD.

The chapter leads to Christ by promise. The land is called Immanuel's in verse 8, and the confession of verse 10, 'God is with us,' stands against every plan of the nations. The Gospel of Matthew returns to the name at its beginning and its end, Matthew 1:23 and 28:20. The one whose land is flooded is the one who will, in the end, bear the flood. He enters the human experience of judgment and darkness, and the cross is the place where those who walk in darkness and the Light who came to them meet.

The chapter leads to Christ by the household of the prophet. Isaiah says, 'I will wait for the LORD, who is hiding His face from the house of Jacob. I will put my trust in Him.' Hebrews takes these words as spoken by Jesus, who shared in the humanity of His children and is not ashamed to call them brothers, Hebrews 2:11-14. The Son who trusted the Father in the hiding of His face on the cross, Matthew 27:46, is the one who stands before God with the children given to Him.

It leads to Christ by the light that comes after the darkness. The closing verse of the chapter, with its anguish, gloom and darkness, is answered at once in Isaiah 9:1-2, and Matthew sees the answer in Jesus's move to Galilee, Matthew 4:13-16. The light does not come to people who sought it; it comes 'on those living in the land of the shadow of death.'

Caution is appropriate. The sealed testimony, the scroll and the child's name do not hide further details of the gospel. The prophetess and her son are not types of Mary and Jesus. The links rest on the New Testament's own quotations: the stone, the trust and the children, and the light.
study.god:
The chapter shows a God who is on both sides of the stone. He is a sanctuary for those who regard Him as holy and a trap for those who do not. This is not a divided character. It is the one holiness meeting two kinds of people. The same truth that comforts the humble offends the proud, and Isaiah does not hide the fact that the LORD is dangerous to be near in the wrong spirit.

He is the God who speaks before He acts. The scroll with a name on it, the reliable witnesses and the dated sign are a way of giving a prophecy in public before it comes true, so that when the plunder of Damascus arrives no one can say it was luck. God provides evidence and does not demand blind faith. In the same way, the testimony of verse 16 is to be bound and sealed, which shows that He is a God who preserves His word for a later day.

He is sovereign over the nations. The Euphrates that rises is 'the king of Assyria and all his pomp,' and the Lord 'will surely bring' it. The nations that huddle together in verse 9 are told that every plan will fail, 'For God is with us.' The chapter does not treat the Assyrian army as a force that has slipped out of control but as a flood that obeys a command. Yet it also does not treat the people as innocent victims. They 'rejected' the gentle water.

He is patient in judgment. The water reaches the neck and not past it. Even in the flood the land is still Immanuel's, and verse 10 says that God is with them. The same God who sends the flood is the God of the promise.

He is a God who hides His face and is still to be trusted. Isaiah says, 'I will wait for the LORD, who is hiding His face from the house of Jacob.' This is an honest statement about the experience of judgment. The LORD's face is turned away, and the prophet does not pretend otherwise, but he trusts and waits. The doctrine of God that comes out of the chapter allows both the hiddenness of God and His faithfulness, and the prophet holds them at once. Deuteronomy 31:17-18 had warned of the hiding of God's face, and Isaiah's response is faith in the God who hides.

He is the one to be feared. 'Only He should be feared; only He should be dreaded.' This is not the terror of a tyrant. It is the awe that makes other fears small, and it is the beginning of wisdom, Proverbs 1:7. Isaiah 33:6 says that 'The fear of the LORD is Zion's treasure.'

For worship, the chapter calls us to put the LORD first in what we take seriously, to prefer His word to every whisper, and to wait. It also leaves us with a plain question about what we regard as holy, since the one who is a sanctuary is also the one who cannot be treated as ordinary.

crossReferences.note: The historical record of Tiglath-pileser's capture of Galilee and the land of Naphtali, with the deportation of its people. It is the fulfilment of the sign of Maher-shalal-hash-baz, and the very region that Isaiah 9:1 names and that Matthew 4:13-16 says Jesus entered.

Ahaz travels to Damascus, sees the altar there and orders Uriah the priest to build a copy. A priest of this name is one of Isaiah's witnesses in 8:2. The passage shows what kind of religion the court practised and suggests why the choice of witnesses would have been hard for the king to answer.

The first meeting of Isaiah and Ahaz at the aqueduct, where Ahaz is told to 'calm down and be quiet.' The gentle waters of Shiloah in 8:6 are the water that Ahaz was inspecting. His refusal of the quiet word of 7:4 is the rejection that 8:6 names.

The LORD lays 'a tested stone, a precious cornerstone, a sure foundation,' and the believer will never be shaken. It is the positive side of the stone of Isaiah 8:14, and the New Testament joins the two in Romans 9:33 and 1 Peter 2:6-8.

Paul explains Israel's failure by saying that they pursued righteousness by works and stumbled over the stumbling stone. He quotes Isaiah 8:14 with 28:16 and applies both to Christ. It is the clearest New Testament use of the chapter.

Peter puts three texts together, Isaiah 28:16, Psalm 118:22 and Isaiah 8:14, to say that Christ is the precious cornerstone to those who believe and a stone of stumbling to those who do not. The treatment of one stone in three Old Testament voices shows how the apostles read the Scriptures together.

Peter takes Isaiah 8:12-13 and applies it to Christians who suffer: do not fear what they fear, and 'sanctify Christ as Lord.' The call to put the LORD first among our fears is carried into the life of the church.

The writer puts Isaiah 8:17 and 8:18 on the lips of Jesus, who is not ashamed to call His people brothers and who shared in their flesh and blood. It shows the prophet and his children as a picture of the Saviour and those He saves.

The law forbids turning to mediums and spiritists, which would defile the person who does. It is the basis for Isaiah's question in 8:19 and shows that the people who consult the dead were doing what the Torah had long prohibited.

The darkness of 8:22 is answered in the next breath. The land of Zebulun and Naphtali, humbled in the past, will be honored, and the people walking in darkness will see a great light. The chapter division hides the fact that these verses belong to a single movement.

Matthew sees Isaiah 9:1-2 fulfilled when Jesus moves to Capernaum in the region of Zebulun and Naphtali. It places the light of Christ in the very place of the Assyrian invasion that Isaiah 8 describes, and closes the long arc from darkness to light.

'By repentance and rest you would be saved; your strength would lie in quiet confidence,' and 'you were not willing.' It is the later statement of the principle behind the gentle waters of Shiloah in 8:6. Quiet trust is God's way, and the people refuse it again and again.

study.oneStory:
Isaiah 8 stands in the story at the point where the covenant people choose a lesser protector. In Eden the first couple took the word of a stranger over God's word and found themselves exposed. In Egypt, Israel was brought out by a strong hand, Exodus 15:1-2, and told that the LORD would fight for them. In Isaiah's day the nation turns to a human empire and to the dead, and the story of the first temptation repeats on the scale of a nation. The flood that rises is the old consequence of the old choice.

The chapter also continues the theme of the remnant and the sign. A few disciples keep the sealed testimony, and a prophet waits with his family. The same pattern appears in Noah's household, in Abraham's tent, and in Elijah's seven thousand. God keeps a people through the time of judgment, and the faith of the few preserves the word until it is vindicated.

What the chapter sets up is the turn to light. The darkness of the last verses has no end in itself, and the next chapter gives the child born to David's throne, the shoot of chapter 11, and the servant of the later chapters. The prophet's decision to wait for the LORD who hides His face is the stance of the whole exile, and it is the stance that, in the end, will be met by the coming of the Light.

In the New Testament the stone is Christ, and the children given to Him are the church. He enters the land of Naphtali and begins to preach, and the people in darkness see a light. Those who stumble over Him do so because they take their security elsewhere, but those who trust Him are put in a sanctuary that cannot be shaken. The words 'God with us' become a name in a manger and a promise on a mountain, Matthew 1:23 and 28:20.

In the new creation the darkness is gone. 'There will be no more night,' and God's people will see His face, Revelation 22:4-5. The hiding of the face that Isaiah endured is over, and the people who once roamed hungry and cursing their king and their God stand in the light of the Lamb. The flood has no place in the city where the river is the water of life, Revelation 22:1, and the stone that some stumbled over is the foundation of the city.

quiz.q: What was the purpose of naming Isaiah's second son Maher-shalal-hash-baz?

options.text: To date precisely how soon Damascus and Samaria's wealth would be plundered by Assyria.
options.note: Verse 4 ties the timeline directly to the child's earliest speech, a very short window, confirmed by later historical events.

options.text: To celebrate a military victory Judah had already won.
options.note: The name anticipates a future conquest by Assyria against Judah's enemies, not a Judahite victory already achieved.

options.text: To honor a foreign king's visit to Jerusalem.
options.note: The naming is tied to prophetic timing of judgment, not diplomatic honor.

options.text: To mark the rebuilding of the Jerusalem temple.
options.note: No temple rebuilding is in view; the sign concerns the fall of Damascus and Samaria.

quiz.q: What does the flood imagery of verses 7-8 depict?

options.text: Assyria overwhelming Judah itself, reaching up to the neck, even though Judah expected Assyria to help against its enemies.
options.note: The address to 'Immanuel' ties this devastation directly to Judah's own land, a sober irony.

options.text: A literal flood of the Jordan River.
options.note: The Euphrates and the king of Assyria are named explicitly; the flood is a metaphor for military invasion.

options.text: The permanent destruction of Assyria by Judah.
options.note: The flood metaphor describes Assyria as the invading force, not Assyria's own destruction.

options.text: A description of agricultural irrigation improvements.
options.note: This is judgment imagery describing invasion, not an agricultural development.

quiz.q: What does verse 13, 'the LORD of Hosts is the One you shall regard as holy,' call God's people to do?

options.text: Fear the LORD alone rather than fearing conspiracy, enemy kings, or circumstances.
options.note: This directly answers the fear driving both Ahaz's unbelief and the general population's anxiety.

options.text: Avoid all forms of fear entirely, including reverence for God.
options.note: The call is to redirect fear toward God alone, not eliminate reverent fear altogether.

options.text: Trust in Assyria as God's appointed protector.
options.note: The whole passage warns against trusting Assyria; the call is to trust the LORD instead.

options.text: Build stronger physical fortifications around Jerusalem.
options.note: The remedy given is spiritual, fearing God alone, not primarily a military engineering solution.

quiz.q: How does the New Testament use the image of the LORD as 'a stone of stumbling' from verse 14?

options.text: Romans 9 and 1 Peter 2 identify Christ Himself as this stone, a sanctuary to believers and a stumbling block to unbelief.
options.note: Both passages quote or allude to Isaiah 8:14 directly in reference to Christ.

options.text: It is never referenced again in the New Testament.
options.note: It is directly quoted in Romans 9:33 and closely echoed in 1 Peter 2:8.

options.text: It refers only to physical stones used in temple construction.
options.note: The New Testament applies the image personally and Christologically, not to literal building materials.

options.text: It describes only Israel's national history with no application to Christ.
options.note: The New Testament explicitly and directly applies this image to Christ's person and the response He provokes.

quiz.q: What standard does verse 20, 'to the law and to the testimony,' establish?

options.text: Any teaching or claim must be tested against God's revealed word, or it has no true light.
options.note: This becomes a timeless principle for discerning truth from error, applied here specifically against consulting mediums.

options.text: Only the priests are permitted to read Scripture.
options.note: The verse calls the whole audience to test teaching against the word, not restrict access to it.

options.text: Legal courts should replace prophetic guidance entirely.
options.note: 'The law and the testimony' refers to God's revealed word, not a call to replace prophecy with civil courts.

options.text: Traditions passed down by elders carry equal authority to Scripture.
options.note: The verse elevates God's own revealed word as the standard, not human tradition as an equal authority.

questions: God dated Assyria's conquests precisely through a child's name, proving His word could be trusted in the short term. Where do you need that same confidence in God's longer-range promises to you?
The people were tempted to fear conspiracies and consult mediums rather than fear God. What anxieties or 'conspiracies' are competing for your fear and attention right now instead of God?

The LORD is a sanctuary to those who trust Him, but a stumbling stone to those who do not. How does that same Christ function as either refuge or offense in your own life depending on your response to Him?
Isaiah bound up the testimony and waited on the LORD even while God was 'hiding His face' from the nation. How do you keep trusting God's word during seasons when He feels distant or silent?
Verse 20 calls for testing every teaching against 'the law and the testimony.' What ideas, fears, or influences in your life right now need to be tested against Scripture rather than simply accepted?

translationNotes.note: Maher-shalal-hash-baz means 'quick to the plunder, swift to the spoil,' an unusually long and dramatic Hebrew name functioning as a walking prophecy of imminent conquest.
The direct address 'O Immanuel' ties this passage back to 7:14, whether read as speaking to the same child or as a poetic title for the land bound up with that name's promise of God's presence.

Consulting 'the spirits of the dead' and spiritists who 'whisper and mutter' reflects known ancient Near Eastern necromancy practices explicitly forbidden in Deuteronomy 18:10-11, here rebuked as an alternative, illegitimate source of guidance in place of God's word.

meta.notes: BSB text fetched from the Makor scripture toolkit for Isaiah 8:1-22.
